Reproducibility

How the fictional data were generated

Batch size is drawn between 1 and 16. Mean minutes equal 20 + 5 × size + 0.18 × size² + 5 × sin(size/3); random noise grows with size. Other transformation examples are separate simulations.

Fixed seed: 440731. Read the complete generator and analysis code; inspect the saved results.

Known truth: The case’s completion-time curve bends as batches grow, and larger batches have more variable completion times. A size-based rule needs a buffer for deadline promises.

These are model assumptions and generated outcomes, not claims about a real population.

Stop 01 / 24

Define the regression question

Juniper is a fictional workshop that assembles reusable sensor crates. The planning question is how completion time changes with batch size. A descriptive curve summarizes this generated population; a prediction estimates time for a new batch; a causal claim asks what would happen if the same operation were assigned a different batch size. These are distinct targets, even when the fitted equation looks identical.

Our unit is one batch. X is standardized crate units and Y is completion minutes. The dataset has 180 independent simulated batches. The observed X range is 1.074 to 15.883. A prediction outside that range is an extrapolation, not additional evidence.

Pause and explain

What must be added before a descriptive slope can justify an operational intervention?

Compare your reasoning
A design and assumptions connecting intervention to outcomes, including treatment definition, confounding, interference and the target population. A good fit alone does not supply them.

Stop 02 / 24

Know what the simulation assumes

X ∼ Uniform(1,16); Z ∼ N(0,1), independent.
Y = 20 + 5X + 0.18X² + 5 sin(X/3) + (3 + 0.35X)Z.

The original generator uses seed 440731. The conditional mean is the deterministic part and the conditional standard deviation grows with X. This lets us distinguish a fitted approximation from a known teaching truth. None of the observations describe a real workshop. The downloadable script generates every row locally before fitting anything.

Pause and explain

Does larger conditional variance change E[Y|X]?

Compare your reasoning
No. The noise has conditional mean zero. Its changing spread affects uncertainty and prediction risk, while the conditional mean is defined by the deterministic part.

Stop 03 / 24

Bin means trade detail for stability

A bin scatter first partitions X, then computes the mean of X and the mean of Y within each interval. It is not a regression on the original rows. Equal-width bins expose uneven occupancy; quantile bins make counts more uniform but change the meaning of horizontal distances. Never silently treat a mean of bin means as the overall mean when counts differ.

These bins all use width 2.5. The boundaries were fixed before examining Y. Rebinning repeatedly until a preferred story appears is a form of specification search.

Pause and explain

What is lost when we retain only the bin means?

Compare your reasoning
Within-bin dispersion, leverage points and nonlinear structure inside each interval. Counts and the original scatter should accompany the summary.

Stop 04 / 24

Use LOWESS as a diagnostic

Our LOWESS implementation fits a weighted line near each evaluation point. It uses the nearest 35% of observations, tricube weights w = [1 − (distance/bandwidth)³]³ inside the neighborhood, and no robust reweighting pass. The local intercept is the plotted estimate. Larger neighborhoods smooth more but can hide genuine curvature; small ones can follow noise.

Pause and explain

Is every wiggle in the smoother a population feature?

Compare your reasoning
No. Sampling noise, bandwidth and edge behavior can all create or erase apparent shape. Compare defensible settings and assess prediction outside the fitted rows.

Stop 05 / 24

Specify the best linear approximation

ŷᵢ = b₀ + b₁xᵢ; (b₀,b₁) = argmin Σᵢ(yᵢ − b₀ − b₁xᵢ)².

The fitted line is ŷ = 17.518 + 7.228X. Its slope is a constant change in predicted minutes per standardized batch unit. The intercept is the line’s value at zero, which lies outside our sampled support. A model can be linear in its coefficients while including X², log X or a hinge as predictors.

OLS targets squared vertical errors in Y, not geometric distance to the line. In the population, the best linear projection need not equal E[Y|X]. Our curved DGP makes that distinction concrete: the line is a useful simplification only for a stated range and loss.

Pause and explain

Does a nonzero intercept imply that an empty batch takes that many minutes?

Compare your reasoning
No. The intercept extrapolates to an unsupported value. A substantive zero-batch claim would require an appropriate process model or data there.

Stop 06 / 24

Reconstruct a five-row fit

b₁ = Σ(xᵢ−x̄)(yᵢ−ȳ) / Σ(xᵢ−x̄)²; b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄.
Independent five-row arithmetic example
XGenerated YFitted YResidual Y − fitted
19.510.300-0.800
215.012.2002.800
311.514.100-2.600
416.016.0000.000
518.517.9000.600

Here x̄ = 3.000, ȳ = 14.100, Sxx = 10.000 and Sxy = 19.000. Dividing gives b₁ = 1.900; substituting gives b₀ = 8.400. Squaring and adding the five residuals gives SSE = 15.600. These rows are newly generated from Y = 7 + 2.5X plus discrete noise, not extracted from the workshop sample.

Pause and explain

Why must the fitted line pass through (x̄,ȳ)?

Compare your reasoning
The intercept normal equation gives Σeᵢ = 0. Therefore ȳ = b₀ + b₁x̄. This is sample algebra when an intercept is included, not evidence that population errors are mean-zero conditional on X.

Stop 07 / 24

Separate identities from assumptions

Xᵀe = 0; with an intercept, Σeᵢ = 0.
Population exogeneity: E[ε|X] = 0 is a separate assumption.

The numerical residual sum is -0.0000000000 and the X-weighted residual sum is -0.0000000000, both zero up to floating-point rounding. OLS makes fitted residuals orthogonal to included regressors even when a relevant variable is omitted. That is why a residual average of zero cannot validate a causal model.

In matrix terms, fitted values project Y onto the column space of the design matrix. Full column rank gives a unique coefficient vector. With exact dependence, fitted values may still be unique while individual coefficients are not.

Pause and explain

Would adding X² allow residuals to correlate with X² after refitting?

Compare your reasoning
With an intercept and full numerical rank, OLS makes the new residuals orthogonal to X² too. This remains an in-sample identity and does not guarantee out-of-sample adequacy.

Stop 08 / 24

Keep three denominators visible

TSS = Σ(yᵢ−ȳ)² = ESS + SSE.
Training MSE = SSE/n; residual variance estimate = SSE/(n−p); sample variance of Y = TSS/(n−1).
Distinct variation summaries
QuantityCalculated valueMeaning
TSS151,299.568Variation around the sample mean
SSE7,382.658Squared fitted misses
ESS143,916.911Fitted variation around the mean
RMSE6.404Minutes, denominator n
Residual SD6.440Minutes, denominator n − 2
Sample variance of Y845.249Minutes squared, denominator n − 1

The unbiased-error-variance interpretation of SSE/(n−p) needs a correct linear mean model and homoskedastic independent errors. Our first case deliberately violates those conditions. The number is still computable, but its classical interpretation is not automatically warranted.

Pause and explain

Can sample SD of Y and training RMSE be used interchangeably?

Compare your reasoning
No. One describes variation before conditioning; the other summarizes fitted prediction errors. They answer different questions and use different denominators.

Stop 09 / 24

Interpret R² without promoting it

R² = 1 − SSE/TSS = 0.9512.
In-sample variation decomposition — chart data
GroupMinutes squared
Explained143917
Residual7382.66

R² is an in-sample proportional reduction in squared deviations relative to the mean-only model. With the same rows, outcome and intercept, adding regressors cannot reduce ordinary R². That makes it a fit summary rather than a complexity-adjusted model-choice rule. Out-of-sample R² may be negative when predictions lose to the declared reference.

R² is not the fraction of outcomes caused by batch size. It is also not directly comparable across different outcome transformations, samples or weights.

Pause and explain

If R² rises when X³ is added, has the model earned deployment?

Compare your reasoning
No. Evaluate the extra flexibility using held-out predictions, a decision-relevant loss and the intended deployment population.

Stop 10 / 24

Read residuals against predictors

A residual is observed minus fitted. Positive means the line underpredicts; negative means it overpredicts. A curved pattern in residuals against X indicates missed mean structure. A fan shape indicates changing spread, although a misspecified mean can also distort apparent variance. A histogram alone collapses away these relationships.

Pause and explain

Could a symmetric residual histogram coexist with a badly wrong mean?

Compare your reasoning
Yes. Positive misses at the ends and negative misses in the middle can yield a symmetric overall distribution while revealing a systematic curve against X.

Stop 11 / 24

Choose the outcome scale deliberately

We now switch to three independent fictional sensor-module experiments so that each functional form has a clear population meaning. They share X ∼ Uniform(1,12), but their outcomes are separately generated. The log-level case uses log Y = 2.8 + 0.11X + Normal(0,0.2²). The level-log case uses Y = 40 + 15 log X + Normal(0,4²). The log-log case uses log Y = 2 + 0.7 log X + Normal(0,0.18²).

A log is appropriate only for strictly positive values with a meaningful ratio interpretation. Adding an arbitrary constant to accommodate zeros changes the estimand and can change conclusions. Explain whether a zero represents absence, censoring, a structural category or a measurement problem before deciding on a model.

Pause and explain

Why not compare all three models using R²?

Compare your reasoning
They describe different generated outcomes and, for two cases, a different scale. Even on one dataset, a log-scale fit statistic does not by itself rank original-scale prediction quality.

Stop 12 / 24

Translate a log-level coefficient

log ŷ = b₀ + b₁X; exact proportional contrast for ΔX: exp(b₁ΔX) − 1.

The fitted log coefficient is 0.11797. A one-unit X increase corresponds to 12.52% in the exponentiated fitted log. The approximation 100b₁% is useful only for small changes. The relationship is multiplicative on the outcome scale even though the predictor is not logged.

Pause and explain

Does this coefficient necessarily describe a proportional change in the arithmetic conditional mean?

Compare your reasoning
Only with an appropriate retransformation factor whose conditional behavior supports that interpretation. A varying error distribution can make the mean ratio differ from exp(b₁ΔX).

Stop 13 / 24

Distinguish median and arithmetic mean

If log Y = m(X) + ε, E[Y|X] = exp(m(X)) E[exp(ε)|X].

Exponentiating a conditional log mean gives a geometric mean. It is also a conditional median when the log error has median zero. It generally does not give the arithmetic mean. For this independent homoskedastic log-normal experiment, a constant factor is justified by the generator. The empirical smearing factor, the average of exp(fitted log residual), is 1.01952.

A global smearing estimate is not a universal correction. If error spread varies with X, estimate a suitable conditional factor or choose another model. For validation, estimate smearing using training residuals only, never the held-out outcomes.

Pause and explain

Should every endpoint of a log prediction interval be multiplied by the mean smearing factor?

Compare your reasoning
No. Quantiles transform monotonically by exponentiation. A correction for an arithmetic mean is a different calculation from transforming predictive quantiles.

Stop 14 / 24

Read a level-log effect in units

ŷ = b₀ + b₁ log X; change from X to rX: b₁ log r.

Here the fitted slope is 14.697. A 10% increase in X gives an exact fitted difference of b₁ log(1.10) = 1.401 output units, regardless of starting X. A one-unit increase in X has a different effect depending on the baseline because the local derivative is b₁/X.

Is a 10% X increase the same as adding 0.10 to log X?

Compare your reasoning
Not exactly. The log increment is log(1.10). Using 0.10 is a small-change approximation, not the exact transformation.

Stop 15 / 24

Interpret elasticity and finite changes

log ŷ = b₀ + b₁ log X; elasticity = b₁.
Exact fitted percentage difference for multiplier r: 100(rᵇ¹ − 1).

The estimated elasticity is 0.69545. A 10% larger input corresponds to 6.85% in the exponentiated fitted outcome. The coefficient is a local percentage response, not a percentage-point change in an outcome rate. For finite changes use the power expression, and state whether you are discussing a median, geometric mean or arithmetic mean.

Pause and explain

If X doubles, should the fitted percent change be reported as 100b₁%?

Compare your reasoning
No. Use 100(2ᵇ¹ − 1). The local derivative interpretation does not turn a large discrete change into a linear percentage shortcut.

Stop 16 / 24

Separate leverage, outliers and influence

Return to Juniper. We append one deliberately constructed stress-test row, X = 35 and Y = 280, far beyond the generated support. Leverage measures how unusual its predictor position is; a residual measures vertical surprise conditional on the fit; influence measures how much an estimate changes when that row is perturbed or removed. They are related but not synonymous.

hᵢ = xᵢᵀ(XᵀX)⁻¹xᵢ; Dᵢ = [eᵢ²/(p s²)] × hᵢ/(1−hᵢ)².

The largest Cook’s distance belongs to row 180 (zero-based): h = 0.204, residual = 7.572 and Cook’s D = 0.222. The original slope is 7.228; with the stress row it is 7.300. These are sensitivity calculations, not a recommended deletion rule.

Pause and explain

Should an influential row automatically be removed?

Compare your reasoning
No. First verify measurement and scope. A valid unusual case may be exactly the case the decision must accommodate. Report sensitivity and justify any sample restriction independently of the preferred result.

Stop 17 / 24

Expose measurement and selection choices

Two new sensitivity calculations use the same workshop outcomes. First, we replace X with X plus independent Normal(0,3²) measurement noise. Second, we retain only rows whose outcome exceeds the sample median. The clean slope is 7.228, the noisy-predictor slope is 4.801, and the selected-sample slope is 7.171 using 90 rows.

Classical attenuation is a population result for a correctly specified linear model with additive independent predictor error; our nonlinear example is only an illustration, not a proof of that formula. Selection on the outcome changes the conditional distribution being studied. A valid numerical domain and absence of missing cells do not establish representative measurement or sampling.

Pause and explain

Does conditioning on high outcomes merely remove “bad data”?

Compare your reasoning
No. It creates a different target population and can alter the relationship between X and errors. State the selection mechanism before interpreting the fitted slope.

Stop 18 / 24

Separate fitting, selection and evaluation

Before the predictive comparison, the lab uses a fixed random split: 135 development rows and 45 final evaluation rows. Candidate specifications are line, quadratic, cubic and a continuous hinge with a predeclared knot at X = 8. Five development folds choose the model by pooled squared prediction error. Only the selected specification receives a final test score.

  • Training rows estimate coefficients.
  • Development validation compares candidates.
  • The held-out final sample audits the frozen procedure.

All shapes and the knot were declared before the comparison. The random split imitates a new independent batch from the same generator. It does not imitate a new factory, a future process change or an extreme-size batch.

Pause and explain

If the final score disappoints, can you select the second-best candidate on that same final sample?

Compare your reasoning
You can diagnose the failure, but selecting again turns that sample into development data. A revised procedure needs a genuinely new final evaluation or another defensible validation design.

Stop 19 / 24

Interpret polynomial terms together

ŷ = b₀ + b₁X + b₂X²; local slope = b₁ + 2b₂X.

The full-sample descriptive quadratic has coefficients 21.69517, 5.97796, 0.07357. At X = 4, 8 and 12, its local slopes are 6.567, 7.155, 7.744 minutes per unit. The linear coefficient alone is the derivative at X = 0, not the model’s general slope. A cubic adds another changing component.

Pause and explain

Does a negative X coefficient imply that increasing X always reduces Y in a quadratic?

Compare your reasoning
No. Evaluate b₁ + 2b₂X over the supported range. Individual polynomial coefficients should not be interpreted as separate additive mechanisms.

Stop 20 / 24

Use a hinge without creating a jump

ŷ = b₀ + b₁X + b₂ max(X−8,0).

The hinge contribution is zero at and below 8, then grows linearly above 8. The fitted descriptive slopes are 6.725 below the knot and 7.629 above it. The coefficient on the hinge is a change in slope, not the upper-segment slope itself. Continuity is built into the basis, while a jump would require an additional indicator.

Pause and explain

Why not average fold RMSEs when fold sizes differ?

Compare your reasoning
Pool squared errors and divide by the total row count, then take one square root. Averaging roots changes the weighting and is not generally the same quantity.

Stop 22 / 24

Audit the frozen prediction procedure

After selecting hinge from development cross-validation, the lab refits that specification on all development rows and scores the untouched 45-row final sample. Its final RMSE is 6.735 minutes. No other candidate is selected or retuned using that score.

This is one random holdout, so uncertainty about generalization remains. The score estimates performance for the same synthetic population and squared-error task, not causal effects or arbitrary transport. More repeated development validation can assess selection stability; a larger untouched sample can improve the precision of final performance estimates.

Pause and explain

May you call this model “validated for all workshops”?

Compare your reasoning
No. The sampling design supports a much narrower statement: estimated prediction performance for new independent batches from this particular generator and supported feature range.

Stop 23 / 24

Choose a model for the actual decision

Under squared loss the optimal population point prediction is E[Y|X]. Under absolute loss it is a conditional median. If late completion is substantially more costly than early completion, an upper conditional quantile may be a better planning target. A model can therefore win one score and be inappropriate for the decision.

A planning recommendation should name the cost of an error, available predictors at the planning moment, supported batch range and fallback for unfamiliar cases. Neither a visually smooth curve nor a high R² establishes these choices. A model that predicts a mean also does not provide a capacity buffer automatically.

Pause and explain

Would adding a fixed safety margin to every mean prediction solve asymmetric risk?

Compare your reasoning
Not generally. Required buffers can vary with conditional dispersion and the cost ratio. Model and validate the relevant quantile or decision rule directly.

Stop 24 / 24

Deliver an auditable regression claim

A defensible handoff says: “For independently generated Juniper batches, we compared four predeclared mean-model forms using five-fold development validation. The hinge specification had the smallest development RMSE. Its frozen final-sample RMSE was 6.735 minutes across 45 rows. These results concern prediction under squared loss within the simulated process, not intervention effects.”

  • Include the unit, outcome, feature availability, generator and seed.
  • Keep sample exclusions, transformations, smearing and knot choices visible.
  • Separate descriptive full-sample figures from held-out prediction evidence.
  • Deliver the executable script, notebook output and calculated results together.

The lab assertions verify the OLS decomposition, normal equations and disjoint final sample. Re-run the notebook from a clean kernel, then change a declared generator assumption and explain which conclusions should survive.

Pause and explain

What is the most important limitation to carry into the next lesson?

Compare your reasoning
The point estimate alone does not describe sampling uncertainty or an individual future outcome. Lesson 5 adds those distinctions and extends conditional comparisons to several predictors.
